title: The 72-Hour Storm Response
summary: Mobilize intelligence, marketing, and boots in the first 72 hours after a hail event — and capture 70% of the available revenue your competitors will miss.
body_markdown:
## The cost of being slow

Storms reward speed and punish hesitation. The companies that mobilize in 72 hours after a Class 4 hail event capture roughly 70% of the available revenue in that zip. The companies that take a week to figure out what to do split the remaining 30% with everyone else.

The difference between those two outcomes isn't talent. It's preparation. The 72-hour playbook is the muscle memory you build in the calm weeks so that when the storm hits, you don't have to think.

This lesson breaks the 72 hours into three blocks: **Intelligence (hours 0–6), Marketing (hours 6–24), and Boots (hours 24–72).**

## Hours 0–6: Intelligence

The storm clears. The radar is empty. Your first move is not to send reps out. It's to know exactly where they should go.

**Pull NOAA hail maps the moment the storm clears.** [nws.noaa.gov](https://www.weather.gov) and SPC reports are free. Look specifically for hail stones ≥1.25 inches in diameter — that's the minimum threshold for confident damage. Anything smaller and you'll burn time on borderline claims.

**Identify the 3–5 hardest-hit zip codes.** Don't try to cover everywhere. Concentration wins in the first wave. Pick the worst-hit zips and put 80% of your effort there for the first week.

**Pull aerial maps for those zips.** Tools like EagleView, Google Earth Pro, or even Zillow give you a quick read on:
- Density of single-family detached homes (your targets)
- Age of construction (10-year-old roofs are jackpot)
- Subdivision boundaries (work block-by-block, not address-by-address)

**Cross-reference your existing customer database.** Past customers in hit zips are your warmest leads. Send them a text — not a sales pitch, just a heads-up. Half of them will ask you to come check their roof.

This whole block is 4–6 hours of work for one person. Do it Saturday morning if the storm hit Friday night. By lunchtime, you know exactly which 4 neighborhoods to attack first.

## Hours 6–24: Marketing

With the storm zones identified, you flip three switches in parallel.

**Switch 1: Pause and re-target paid campaigns.** Pause every campaign outside the storm zip. Re-allocate that budget to Meta and Google ads geofenced to the affected zips. The creative is simple: "Free 60-second storm damage check — same day available." Landing page is a calendar booking form, nothing else. Don't send people to your homepage. Send them to a one-purpose page that books an inspection.

**Switch 2: Launch a postcard drop.** Postcards still work for storm. They are not optional. Mail to the top 3 zips with a 4x6 card that says: roof inspection, photos in your hand, storm-specific, free. Get them in the mail within 48 hours. ROI is typically 4–8x in the first 30 days.

**Switch 3: Update your Google Business Profile.** Post a storm-response update. Pin it. Add a photo of your crew in the field with a clipboard (not on a roof — that signals "sales," not "inspection"). Update your services to highlight "storm damage inspections."

If your aaron.chat marketing partner is already running, all three of these get done by them in parallel while you focus on the team. If you're running marketing yourself, block 4 hours on day 1 for these three switches and don't be interrupted.

## Hours 24–72: Boots

Now the reps go out.

**Deploy in pairs.** Solo canvassing is for veterans. New reps work in pairs — one knocks, one observes and provides cover for safety and morale. The pair does 100–120 doors per day combined. Solo veteran reps can do 150+.

**Use the 7-Question Storm Knock from day 1.** Don't let reps freelance during a storm — that's how reputation gets burned. Run the script. The script works. We'll cover it in detail in Lesson 3.

**Target: 1 inspection booked per 8 doors knocked.** That's the benchmark in active storm territory. If a rep is below 1 in 12, get them off the street and review their first 20 knocks with you on a video call. Something is broken.

**Inspect within 24 hours of booking.** Speed wins the claim because adjusters get assigned chronologically. The homeowner who files Tuesday morning gets a Friday adjuster slot. The homeowner who files Friday afternoon gets a slot 12 days later — by which time the homeowner has heard from 4 other contractors and forgotten which one they liked.

**Set up the war room.** Owner, sales manager, and one ops person. 8am stand-up every morning for the first two weeks. Three questions only: How many doors yesterday? How many inspections booked? What's the blocker?

## Days 4–14: Compound

The 72-hour playbook gets you to launch. The next 11 days are where revenue compounds.

**File every claim within the first week.** Adjusters get backed up after week 2. A claim filed on day 3 gets an adjuster on day 10. A claim filed on day 10 gets an adjuster on day 30. Speed compounds.

**Send 'I was your neighbor' letters to non-openers.** Every door that didn't open gets a letter within 48 hours. Personal handwriting on the envelope. Inside: a printed photo of your crew on the block, the address of the neighbor whose roof you just inspected (with permission), and a number to call. This converts 2–4% of non-opens into bookings — pure incremental revenue from doors you'd already given up on.

**Be at every adjuster appointment.** Period. The adjuster meeting is where supplements get won or lost. A rep with photos and a tablet at the meeting consistently gets 20–40% more scope than a rep who skips it. Your time is best spent in those meetings, not on more doors.

**Track the funnel in CRM.** Every lead moves through the same stages: door knocked → inspection booked → inspected → claim filed → adjuster scheduled → claim approved → contract signed → installed. If your CRM doesn't track these stages, your CRM is wrong and you're flying blind. Fix it before the next storm.

## What you should expect

If you execute the full 72-hour play after a Class 4 hail event in a 50,000-population city, the realistic outcome is:

- **80–150 inspections** in the first 30 days
- **40–80 claims filed**
- **25–50 signed contracts**

That is roughly $400K–$750K in committed revenue, from a single storm, if you move fast.

The companies that don't have this playbook get 5–15 jobs out of the same storm and call it a good month. The difference between those two outcomes is the 72 hours.

## The night you build the playbook

The last thing on this lesson: you don't build this playbook the night the storm hits. You build it tonight, when the sky is clear.

Write the storm checklist. Save your NOAA bookmarks. Pre-draft your geofenced ad copy. Pre-design your postcard. Set the war room schedule. Print the script.

When the alarm goes off, the difference between winning and losing is whether you scramble or execute. Build it now so you only execute later.
key_takeaways: Storms reward speed. 70% of revenue belongs to whoever moves in 72 hours.
Hours 0–6: intelligence. NOAA maps, top 3 zips, aerial scouting.
Hours 6–24: marketing. Geofenced ads, postcards, GBP update.
Hours 24–72: boots in pairs, 100+ doors/day, 7-Question Knock only.
File every claim week 1. Adjuster queues back up by week 2.

scripts.name: Existing-customer storm text
scripts.when_to_use: Within 6 hours of the storm clearing, to every past customer in the affected zip codes.
lines: Hey [first name] — Tyler with Roof Pitcher.
Just checking — heard the storm Tuesday had hail in your area.
If you want me to swing by for a free 60-second roof check this week, reply and I'll text you a time slot.
Either way, hope you and the family are good.

scripts.name: Neighbor-letter opener (non-opens, day 3-5)
scripts.when_to_use: Hand-addressed envelope mailed to homes that didn't answer the door during the first canvass.
lines: I knocked Tuesday afternoon and you weren't home — I didn't want to leave a flyer.
I just finished inspecting [neighbor's address — with their permission] and found significant hail damage.
If you want a free 60-second check on yours, my direct number is [###-###-####]. No sales call, just a roof inspection.

quiz.q: What is the minimum hail size that justifies confident damage and active mobilization?
quiz.explanation: Below 1.25 inches you'll burn time on borderline claims. 1.25 inches is the operational threshold.

quiz.q: How many storm zip codes should you concentrate effort on in the first week?
choices: Every affected zip in a 100-mile radius
Whichever zip is closest to the office
quiz.explanation: Concentration wins in the first wave. 3–5 zips lets you saturate before competitors get organized.

quiz.q: Why does filing a claim in week 1 beat filing it in week 2?
choices: Insurance gives a discount for early filing
Adjusters are assigned chronologically — week-1 filings get earlier appointments
Damage is more visible in week 1
quiz.explanation: Adjuster queues back up fast. Week-1 filings get appointments inside 10 days; week-2 filings often wait 30+.

quiz.q: Where should a sales manager's time most pay off after day 4?
choices: Attending adjuster meetings to win supplements
Reviewing rep ride-alongs at the office
quiz.explanation: Adjuster meetings drive 20–40% more scope. That ROI beats every other hour a manager could spend.

homework: Tonight, write a one-page Storm Response Checklist. Bookmark the NOAA SPC report. Pre-draft your geofenced ad copy. Print one copy and put it in every truck. You will be glad when the alarm goes off at 3am.
